speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege today to say to the house that I hope in my ten and a half years as a member I may have made some responsible contribution to the annals of this historic parliamentary institution. I should like to thank every member in every part of the house for their co-operation and for the friendly associations I have had during this time.
I wish also, Mr. Speaker, to express my gratitude for the co-operation of departmental officials and of every staff member of the House of Commons, as well as recognizing the co-operation of members of the press gallery. Last but not least, Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank you for the tolerance and patience as well as the courtesies you have extended to me.
May I hope for future blessings on this great country and on all those who work with pride and dedication for its future. And now, Mr. Speaker, I bid you all au revoir.

Mr. Chairman, since 1948 the federal government has been giving assistance to the operators of gold mines considered uneconomical under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act.

Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act extended for a period of four years, that is until December 31, 1967. Therefore, it is urgent to introduce today a new amendment.
Last year, during the winter, and quite recently, the government undertook to review the situation in order to know whether the legislation which we are dealing with today was still necessary, in what terms, at what price and at what level of subsidy.
The representations made by the gold producers, by mining associations and delegations from the mining municipalities concerned, in Quebec and Ontario in particular, have been of great assistance to us in carrying out that review, and we wish to thank the groups that came forward.

Excitement and romanticism have been associated with the early development in Canada of the gold mining industry. In the last century placer gold was found in the Cariboo district of British Columbia and in the Klondike in the Yukon. I was in the Yukon recently to visit the latest mining development and spent some time in and around Dawson City, where my grandfather lived at the time of the rush and where he died some 20 years after. It is unbelievable that gold should still be extracted from these same sands.
In the early part of this century, Mr. Chairman, lode gold-that is gold found in hard rock-was discovered and developed at Kirkland Lake, Timmins, Val d'Or, Malartic, Red Lake, Yellowknife and other places. The gold mining industry was a pioneer in the development of much of Canada's north. It became a major element in our mining industry, and gold had the greatest value of any metal mined in Canada for three decades following 1920. The year 1941 was the year of greatest production. In that year the industry produced about 5.3 million ounces, worth about $206 million. At that time the total value of mineral production in Canada was about $560 million; so $206 million for gold alone out of just over half a billion, gives a good indication of the importance of gold mining in those years.
Following world war II, however, the rate of expansion of the whole mineral industry in Canada increased, slowly at first but then more and more rapidly. By 1966 the mineral industry had become a giant in this country, with a total production of slightly over $4 billion. Unfortunately gold mining did not participate in the post-war expansion to the

I understand that my hon. friend the hon. member for Villeneuve will probably have something to say about the "stability" of the price of gold.
Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, few new discoveries were made, and gold mines were forced to rely mainly on known ore zones and their possible extension for their production.
It should be added here that the industry undertook to increase its efficiency by the use of improved mining equipment and methods. The effort achieved a marked degree of success. For a few years total output of gold in Canada increased. It reached a post-war high in 1960 when a total of about 4.6 million ounces was produced having a value of about $157 million. However, the improvement in efficiency has not prevented many gold mines from closing in the last few years due to depletion of ore reserves through exhaustion, and again due to increasing costs.

As an aside I might say that lode gold mines bring out the gold found in hard rock. A small quantity of gold is still recovered in Canada from placer deposits in the beds of streams and rivers, a type of operation almost entirely confined to British Columbia and the Yukon. As a third source gold is also produced as a byproduct from some base metal mines. The subsidy is not paid in that case.

At this stage, Mr. Chairman, I may add right away that gold production remains an important element of our mining industry. It has had its set-backs, it now has problems, but it is not moribund. In 1966, about 3.3 million ounces of gold were produced in Canada, that is a value of $125 million. Gold ranks fifth for value in the list of metals produced in Canada in 1966.
Outside of the U.S.S.R., whose production is not known, Canada ranks second amongst gold producers in the world, immediately after the Union of South Africa-although a good deal behind-since it produces some 30 million ounces.

I should like to say a few words now about gold mining communities. There is an old saying that "gold is where you find it." It was found in many out of the way places in Canada-at least they were remote at the time of the discovery and development of the gold mines. The pioneering role of the mining prospectors and operators was shared by those who came to work in the mines and to provide the services needed in any community. Schools, churches and hospitals were built, as well as homes and business premises; water and power systems were installed, and streets and roads constructed.
There are 20 communities in Canada whose economic support is derived almost entirely from the operation of gold mines. We have estimated that in 1966 the population of these communities exceeded 80,000. This social factor represents, of course, the major cause for the present legislation, as it did for the legislation introduced a few months ago in connection with the Cape Breton coal mines. The discovery and development in recent years of deposits of base metals and industrial minerals has added some economic support to the mining communities of Timmins, Kirkland Lake, Val d'Or and Malartic. Everyone here has heard about the Texas Gulf Sulphur zinc-copper mine at Timmins, the Jones and Laughlin iron ore mine at Kirkland Lake and the pulp mill of Domtar Limited situated about 100 miles north of Val d'Or. The federal Department of Industry has provided financial incentives to new manufacturing and processing industries in designated areas under its area development program. Some success has been achieved through these efforts.
Notwithstanding some diversification of the base, the gold mining communities continue to be dependent mainly on the economic support provided by the operating gold mines. As the gold mines have reduced the scale of their operations or have ceased production, former employees have faced the problem of finding new jobs. The federal Department of Manpower and Immigration has assisted in placing workers in suitable jobs through the Canada manpower centres. Workers are retrained where necessary. They are also given assistance to move to other areas under the manpower mobility program.
Everybody understands that moving is a difficult operation in the case of people who have grown up in certain areas and who are very much sentimentally attached to those areas, and sympathizes with those who have do do so. Governments try to cushion the shock.
Perhaps I should say something now about the role of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. The act was passed in 1948, at which time a large number of gold mines were faced with operating losses because of increasing costs of production. The operators were, of course, unable to increase the selling price of their product.
Without assistance the mines would have been forced to close. Extensive economic and social dislocations would have followed the abrupt closure of so many mines. The purpose of the legislation was to extend the life of the gold mines and thereby allow their dependent communities to adjust gradually to

The only incentive that the Canadian people have had in the use of many of these private pools of money that are available has been the fact that if you buy a mining stock there is some hope you may make some money which will be tax free. Mr. Chairman, we have before us legislation to extend the provisions of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act for another three years. The 
DEBATES	September 29, 1967
minister has made it very clear that there are to be no other alterations in this legislation involving this field. This morning he used a word, possibly inadvertently, that could well apply to this legislation when he stated that its purpose was to retard the closing of the mines, or something to that effect. I think the word "retardation" is very appropriate to this legislation which has been on the statute books for some 19 years. It is retarding legislation, and according to the minister its purpose is to retard the inevitable.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
I believe the original purpose and intent of the act with which we are dealing today was to foster and maintain the gold mining communities. As we look over the record of what has transpired in the 19 years since this legislation was first enacted we can see what a complete and shoddy failure the act has been in light of the purposes for which it was originally intended. This morning the minister gave a very good outline of the history of the gold mining industry since the act first came into being. It is a history of bankruptcy of ideas and the failure of the policies of the governments of this country over the past 19 years with regard to the gold mining industry. This is what it has been and this is all that it has been-a history of bankruptcy and failure.
The act has not done the job it was originally intended to do. It has been extended from year to year. The very name of the bill should make us realize what a complete failure it has been. Twenty years later it is still called the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. How long does an emergency exist and when do we stop trying to fool ourselves?
The minister mentioned some of the statistics contained in the report of the administration of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1966. We see, for example, that in the first year subsidies were paid, 1948, there were some 117 mines which received assistance from the federal government and in the next year, 1949, there were 122. In 1949, when the highest number of mines was being assisted by the federal government, they received some $12,571,456.90 in assistance from the Canadian taxpayers. By 1965 this number had dropped to 41 but they still received approximately the same amount, $12,053,385. What this really means is that while the contribution by the Canadian taxpayers to this industry has remained practically constant throughout these 19 years, the number
September 29, 1967	COMMONS
of mines participating in the plan has dropped from 122 to 41, which leads us to wonder what assistance this has been to the gold mining communities since this has been the purpose of the act since it was passed in 1948.
I should like to be even more specific by illustrating a situation with which I am very familiar. The Hollinger mine in Timmins has been the biggest gold producer in the Timmins area and in fact has been the second largest gold producer in the world over the past quarter of a century at least. Since 1948 the Hollinger mine has received in subsidies from the Canadian taxpayers some $19,771,145.93, according to the information in the blue book we have here. This includes their three properties, the Hollinger mine at Timmins, the Ross mine at Holtyre and the Young-Davis mine at Matachewan which has been closed down for some years.
We have been notified that within the next year or possibly 18 months the Hollinger mine will be closed down. Therefore we have a situation about which I am well aware. Miners who have worked in the Hollinger mine, some of them for 40 or 45 years, are being thrown out without a pension of any kind. They are being tossed out like an old pair of shoes that one tosses in the garbage can, in spite of the fact that the Canadian taxpayer over the past 18 years has paid $19,771,145.93 to this one company.
How effective has this act been? What have we accomplished? I wonder just how much thought parliament, this government, the government which preceded it and the previous Liberal government have given to the administration of the act, because some very strange things come to the surface if one studies it at all. For example, most of us are quite aware that in 1953 there was a great strike in the gold mines. All the mines in the Timmins area were out of operation for periods varying between five months and seven months. I do not remember the exact date but I believe the Hollinger mine was out of operation for about six months that year.
If we look at this book, keeping in mind that the report is really for the previous year's operations we And that the year before this strike and the year after it the taxpayers of Canada paid a subsidy to this company of $665,908.59 just in respect of the Timmins operation alone but that for the year 1953 when the mine was closed down for six months, when the miners did not draw wages and the community did not receive the benefit of their wages for six months, the
DEBATES	2663
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act taxpayers paid the Hollinger mine $1,012,139.49. Without making a deep study one has to assume that it was a very profitable venture for the Hollinger mine to allow those men to be out on strike for six months because its subsidy from the Canadian taxpayers doubled for that year.
This is just an illustration of why I am trying to make the point that the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act has never been a solution to the problems of the gold mining industry. Apparently it never was intended to be that but rather a gesture to try to fool the public. By dipping into the taxpayers' pockets for the last 20 years governments have been able to maintain this gesture which has solved nothing. The minister said today, supported by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, that there is no future for the gold mining industry. The legislation is just a palliative so that the old pensioner who we know will die within a few years will have a little pittance to make things easier for him until he gasps his last breath.
The legislation the minister is presenting today is for the purpose of extending the act for three years. He gives no particular reason for setting that period. If we look at the history we find that over the past 18 years the mines have closed at the rate of five a year. All he had to do to look after the situation was to extend the act for 18 years, because there will be no communities left if we continue the same policy that has been followed in the past. The minister and the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka have both subscribed today to the idea, which unfortunately has been promoted and sponsored by the Minister of Finance, that gold is of no more good to the world and that we should get rid of it as quickly, decently and quietly as we can. I do not agree with that theory, Mr. Chairman.

I understand that the Minister of Finance at the present time is attending a meeting of the International Monetary Fund, and if we can believe the newspaper reports the major objective of that meeting is to find some substitute for gold to be used as the medium of international exchange.
Let me remind the minister that if we make a study of history we will find that for 5,000 years people have been looking for a substitute for gold but for 5,000 years have been unsuccessful in finding one with any lasting value. I predict without one shred of hesitation that their efforts will be as unsuccessful this time as they have been for the past 5,000 years.
Gold is something we have in Canada which very few countries in the world have today and it is something that is sought for by every country in the world. It is something that is always going to have a sales value because it is one commodity that over the centuries has been accorded the complete trust and confidence of nations all over the world. By pursuing such a policy as the government are pursuing at the present time they are, in my opinion, following a course which is complete idiocy.
The minister pointed out in his speech that there have been no new discoveries of gold. This is not really true. There are new discoveries, some of which I know of myself. There have been new discoveries of gold but they will not be promoted or exploited at this time as long as we have a fixed price that bears no sensible relationship to the value of money today. They will not be exploited or developed as long as the government continues the policy announced by the Minister of Finance of attempting to replace gold with some kind of funny money.
We have noticed over the past 20 years that the number of gold mines in this country has decreased from some 250 to about 30. As I mentioned earlier, at the rate they are being operated they may last for another five to ten years and that will be the end of gold mining until such time as world events catch up to us. But then, after great stress and strain and possibly another depression like we had in the 1930's, gold will come back into

Mr. Chairman, the hon. minister has stressed the importance, for the government, of providing assistance to northwestern Quebec and northeastern Ontario with respect to gold mining. It is common knowledge that these Canadian areas had gold mining developments which, unfortunately, had to be closed down. Recently, I read in the August 1967 issue of a Montreal periodical, La Prosperity, vol. V, no. 1, a greatly significant article.
The mining industry has been for the last 30 years the backbone of the economy in this area. Apart from the Mattagami and Chibougamau developments, located 185 and 330 miles respectively from Rouyn, there is a drastic curtailing of mining production,

Thus, in the area of Val d'Or, several gold mines, namely East Sullivan and Sullivan Consolidated, have almost ceased all production. The Malartic mines have slowed down production.

There also mines have been closed.
In Rouyn-Noranda, the problem is just as acute. Over the years, Noranda has become the reduction centre of copper concentrates of northwestern Quebec and northern Ontario. Now, among the twenty copper producers sending their copper concentrates to Noranda to be reduced, several will stop their shipments shortly, including the Beau-chemin family mines. The prospects are not bright as far as the prosperity and labour market are concerned in that region because with the exception of the mines, there is no secondary industry there. A few years ago we should have had, for instance, the zinc refinery which was set up in the Valley field area instead to process the ores coming from Noranda or northwestern Quebec.
This zinc refinery employing possibly more than a thousand men should have been established in the northwest-this industry belongs to our area-but no government, federal or provincial, has intervened nor asked the Noranda Mines Co. to set up this secondary industry in the area where the ore is mined. No! The plant was allowed to go to Valleyfield, where there is neither copper nor zinc.
There is neither zinc nor copper in Montreal and the suburbs, on St. Catherine Street, but that is the spot decided upon to set up a secondary industry.
Thus, the prospects are not very gay and, within five years, we will have large scale lay-offs at the Noranda Mines whose resources are not eternal.
Mr. Chairman, I say we must support this resolution with all our might to maintain the assistance to the gold mines and I say that, in the circumstances, we should improve such assistance in view of the fact that there are no other industries in our area to give work to our manpower which is being displaced or laid off every day.

We have tremendous potential. For instance, it is well known that between La Sarre, Rouyn-Noranda, Amos or Val d'Or, towards James Bay, there are untold riches, invaluable wealth, but no one in the past 15 or 20 years has thought of a way to ensure their development.

The gold mining industry of Canada finds itself in a paradoxical position. On the one hand the world is short of gold and on the other the gold which lies in our mines in Canada is going to waste while the government in Ottawa does not appear to be doing much about it.
I was astonished by the minister's complete lack of interest in the whole subject. He rose in his place and mechanically presented a proposition to extend the provisions of the act for another three years. He stumbled over a few statistics and then gave the industry the kiss of death by saying that the only reason for the extension of the legislation was to allow gold mining to die gracefully.
I come from a riding which has 90 per cent of the placer gold producers in Canada. The placer gold production of Canada may be relatively small. During his statement the minister repeatedly made the point that the cost of the administration of this act was $231 million. I would point out that production in the Yukon in the first few years at the turn of the century more than equalled the cost of the administration of the act since its inception. The minister has kindly sent me the statistics for which I asked in respect of placer mining. In 1948, of 30 such mines 20 were in the Yukon; in 1950, of the 24 that were operating in Canada 19 were in the Yukon; in 1955, of the 22 operating mines 17 were in the Yukon; in 1960, of the total of 26, 20 were in the Yukon. The total the minister has supplied for 1965 is 22 with no figure given for the number of operators in the Yukon, but I dare say it remains at 19 or 20.
If he looks at the annual report for the year ended March 31, 1966 the minister will find that, throughout all those years, of the total applications for assistance under the act

about one third in number came from people who conduct placer mining operations in the Yukon. Indeed, the largest placer mining operation which existed in Canada until 1966 was that of the Yukon Consolidated Gold Corporation.
This brings me to a point which the minister made. He made special reference to manpower and the high cost of labour. This is indeed a problem not only in the gold mining industry but throughout the mining industry generally. Rather than offer the incentives which are offered with regard to manpower mobility the minister might be well advised to try to convince his colleagues that there is a desparate need for the training of miners in this country. United Keno Hill Mines Limited in the Yukon has drastically curtailed its operation, not because the company was running out of good ground but because it could not meet the labour requirements of the operation, partly on account of the high cost and partly-and this is the point I am now making-because of the unavailability of skilled miners. This is a problem which confronts the whole of the industry.
The solution proposed by the minister is to close down the mines, extend the period of assistance for another three years and perhaps for a further three years, and then let the industry die a graceful death. He seemed to be entirely disinterested in the fiscal ramifications involved. I tried to get the minister to say whether or not he was in favour of increasing the price of gold. He ducked that question. In fact, he went on record as saying, not once but twice, that the gold mining operators who had made representations to the government agreed with him that there was no hope for an increase in the price of gold.
This left me with the impression that no representations for an increase in the price of gold had been made to him. However, in the brief submitted by the gold mining communities comprising some 35 communities in Canada, supported by the regional economic council of northwest Quebec, supported by the association of mining municipalities of northern Ontario and by the northwestern Ontario development council and co-ordinated by the department of industry for the town of Timmins, recommendations in this regard come through loud and clear. They have said on page 4 of their submission, and I think it is worthwhile to put it on the record, that they want a revaluation of the world's currencies in terms of gold under the

Recently there have been some signs of encouragement with the finding of asbestos 40 miles away, but that is quite a distance from the municipality. While we can mobilize relocation of manpower in areas like Cape Breton when an economic problem occurs that requires the closing of a coal mine, it is pretty difficult to mobilize the relocation of a whole municipality. This is what the government is confronted with in connection with places like Dawson City. When gold mining does move out of that area, although certainly it has by no means left yet because we still have a number of small placer operations supporting this and other communities in the Yukon, then the situation will reach the stage where other devices will have to be found to maintain the municipality.
Unlike the previous government, certain of whose tourist investments in that area were scoffed at and scorned by hon. members opposite when they sat on this side of the chamber, this government is displaying remarkably little interest in that kind of direction to the type of community that suffers as the result of the falling off of the mineral industry, in this case the gold mining industry. The minister's colleague, the hon. member for the Northwest Territories, will tell him that the whole northern area of Canada is a mecca for tourists from all over North America. Therein lies a treasure house for the federal government in tourist dollars if it would but realize it.

With respect to exploration I would also point out there is seldom a prospector who does not go out into the bush with a gold pan in his pack. Surely it cannot be against the interests of this country to find more gold mines. If that be the case then I must be more lacking than I thought I was in my appreciation of the value of gold and of the economic need of this country to have it. To be confronted on top of all these problems facing the gold mining industry with recommendations that have the possibility of acceptance, such as those contained in the Carter report is just about putting the last nail in the lid of the coffin of the mining industry as a whole and particularly the gold mining industry.
The minister made certain remarks about a lack of new discoveries. The hon. member for Timmins brought him up short on that and, incidentally, also criticized the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka for not offering policies although he himself did not make one single constructive suggestion to meet the problems. Discovery Mines in the Yukon is one such new find which produced gold for a few months and then had to close down because of problems of high cost.
The whole mining industry in the Yukon, let alone the gold mining industry, operates in a very high cost area. The same situation prevails in the Northwest Territories. There the mining industry also has its problems. Not only mines but individuals are met with almost prohibitive costs in almost every sector of consumer demand and the consumer dollar.
The other day we had a debate on housing. Every house built in the Yukon for miners costs 30 per cent to 40 per cent more than a similar house in Calgary, Edmonton, Ottawa or Toronto. This is the kind of factor that should be taken into consideration when applying legislation of this nature to areas of this kind.
I say to the minister that he should take an adamant stand with his cabinet colleages and insist that the Carter report recommendation that the three year tax exemption period on new mines be abolished be flatly rejected. If he does so he will find 100 per cent support from the mining industry as a whole. I also suggest to him that he should impress upon his colleagues the need for flatly rejecting the Carter report recommendation with respect to depreciation and capital cost allowances. He will also receive 100 per cent support for that stand from the mining industry.

I thank members of the committee for their indulgence. Until the minister convinces his colleagues, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the Minister of Public Works, and all the other federal authorities of whom there are legions, who are poking their noses into the various aspects of the economic fibre of the north, that measures must be taken to reduce the cost of transportation, housing, communication, and all the other myriads of areas where the federal government insists upon jurisdiction, he will have to be continually involved with legislation of this kind. If he expects the mining industry to be a viable self-supporting industry then, in my humble opinion, there must be a reduction of the costs which make this kind of legislation necessary and an endorsement of the kind of recommendation the gold mining communities presented to him in 1966 with regard to the price of gold. Therein, it seems to me, lies the first step in the proper direction toward curing the high cost of living, the high taxes, and the high cost of production in the gold mines generally.
It is only by taking this kind of position, I suggest, that the minister can come anywhere close to solving the problem. It is not one of allowing the industry to die. That is the impression we all received from the minister's remarks. The industry, far from being supported and far from being looked at as an industry which must be arrested in its downward trend, should be looked at as an industry which should attract attention with the ultimate objective of making it a viable, healthy, self-supporting industry. This cannot be done by the sort of negative approach the minister seems to be taking.

Mr. Chairman, earlier today the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources made official his announcement that there would be a three year extension of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act which, in effect, will permit the gold mining companies and communities to exist for another three years. As we heard earlier, in the past
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act year we have had representations from the gold mining communities, The Mining Association of Canada, the unions and others, asking the minister to make a statement which would set at ease those who are involved in the program in these various areas.
I expect that today's announcement, which has been public knowledge for a few days, will have removed some anxiety from the minds of the people in the groups concerned. It is a long awaited statement and one which possibly treats the top of the problem but not necessarily the root of it. We have heard the various members who have spoken here today mention the problems facing the gold mining industry in Canada. We have heard that it is the only commodity in this country in respect of which prices have been fixed since 1935. It would be redundant for me to talk about the problem producing a product on which the price is fixed and the costs are moving up all the time.
I should like to think for a moment that possibly part of the history of our Canada, our west and our north is based on gold. We heard the hon. member for the Cariboo talk about the exciting days when gold was discovered in the Cariboo. We have heard the hon. member for the Yukon talk about the Klondike. When I was a youngster acting as a caddy carrying golf clubs around a gold golf course, I recall carrying the golf bag of a famous Klondiker, Mike Mahoney, the man whom they say carried a piano over the Chilkoot Pass.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Mike was a fantastic person. He started mining with real interest in the Klondike. I think it is an historical fact, as pointed out by the hon. member for the Yukon, that he made a contribution to the growth and development of Canada to the extent of hundreds of millions of dollars.
At this stage we are confronted with a problem which has social and economic implications. We can go back for a considerable period of time to ascertain the effects of the closing of mines in western Quebec, northern Ontario, in the Yukon and in the Northwest Territories. We know there are plans on the part of governments, past and present, to step in at an appropriate time and provide some form of assistance if and when these communities are closed. I wonder if this is really good enough in light of present circumstances.

I have listened to various views expressed here today to the effect that we are not getting to the real root of the problem of gold mining in Canada. We have talked about the problems of manpower in terms of keeping the industry going. In my constituency, our two major mines are operating at 60 per cent capacity because of the lack of miners. It is not difficult to find men to work on the surface or in other capacities in the mill, but it is virtually impossible to find men who will go underground and mine in the true sense of the word.
Perhaps one reason for this difficulty relates to the development of our affluent society in which it is easier to make $600 or $700 per month working in some other line than it is to make $1,100 or $1,200 per month underground. At the same time, I am wondering whether we are missing an opportunity to employ our indigenous people to a greater extent in the production of gold. This suggestion is not really related to the question of increasing the assistance to gold mines, but it does seem to offer some solution to our problem.
I am thinking particularly of the nickel mine at Rankin Inlet in the Northwest Territories where approximately 125 trained miners were released when the mine ran out of economic ore. We have not taken the opportunity to transfer these miners to other communities. This is true to a lesser degree of the Eskimo people working in northern Manitoba. At one time there were between 25 and 30 employed in Yellowknife. Unfortunately, it was difficult to arrange for these people to participate in community life and own their own homes rather than renting houses which were substandard. It was difficult for their wives to become accepted in the community and learn to help in a modem metropolis. This is only part of the problem.
The only way we, as a nation, can determine whether we want this industry to continue is by examining the total effect of gold mining on our national economy. Such a study has not been made. It would include gathering information as to the total amount of bullion produced annually over the last 50 years, the effect of wages paid from the mining operation, the number of service industries and other individuals who depend upon gold mines for their livelihood. We should also consider the taxes paid by mining operations, as well as the personal income taxes paid by the miners and those in associated and related industries. We must also take into account the sales tax paid by the miners and

service industries such as aircraft companies, supply organizations and drilling companies.
Such a study should also cover the foreign exchange picture and the importance of gold to the national economy as well as the effect the profits of gold mining operations have upon further mineral development. I have in mind particularly the COMINCO operation which has spent a great deal of money in the Northwest Territories as a result of their mining operations in Yellowknife. That company has spent a great deal of money on exploration.
It is my feeling that we should also take a look at practices in other countries such as the United States, not only in terms of monetary and fiscal policy, but also to determine what practices are followed by that particular government.
May I ask the hon. member a question at this point? Will he state for the record whether he is in favour of keeping the price of gold at $35 per ounce or increasing it?

I can answer this question in two ways, and if you will bear with me for a few moments my feeling will become obvious to you. Perhaps, you have already made an assumption.
I should like to place on record a portion of an article which appeared in the September 18, 1967 edition of Newsweek. This article reflects to a certain extent the United States viewpoint. The article is entitled "Golden Harvest", and that does not refer to grain from the prairies. It states:
The government's search for new gold resources is beginning to pay off.
Recent underwater finds off the coast of Alaska have been described by Department of Interior officials as "better than we dared hope for".
New sampling techniques, they say, "are hitting the target every time".
Land-based efforts in Nevada have produced new ways to extract gold from low-grade ores. Mines not used because of the high cost of conventional methods may start producing again.
The final paragraph covers a subject about which I intend to find out more. It states:
Note: The government will soon announce a program to bankroll seekers of gold and other scarce minerals. It will boost its share of their costs from the present 50 per cent to a ratio of 75-25.
My point is that we should attempt to get the minister to undertake a study of the effect of this industry on the national economy. We have done this before in this country

in respect of other industries. We have heard figures that there are approximately 12,000 people employed in the industry, and I think such a study would be worthwhile. If you refer to information provided by the department, you find there are approximately 130,000 Canadians directly dependent on gold mining.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR INCREASES IN POSTAL RATES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since I took over my responsibilities as Postmaster General, 21 months ago, the admiration I have for the department has tremendously increased. The system of communications thus made available to the country is a sort of cement which keeps together the bricks of the business world and the individuals.
The Post Office Department, as a government concern, has never been intended to be a profit-making concern-and my own research on the subject supports this. But the Canadian post office has never been intended either to operate at a loss. In other words, the ideal situation would be for the post office to maintain from one year to the other a fair balance between revenues and expenditures.
That ideal situation has been achieved nearly all the time. But, that rule of balance must not overshadow the obligation of the Post Office Department to contribute to the progress of Canada, to the daily life of its people and to the prestige of our country in the world.
That obligation, has also been assumed by the post office. The various branches of the department reach the most remote areas of the country. The speed with which mail is carried within Canada is an example to other postal administrations of the world, and the flow of printed matter which is carried by the post office is a credit to Canada, v/ithin its boundaries as well as abroad.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)

The resolution which has been placed before the house is designed to do four things. I know that some of them will not be popular but I assure the house that the legislation is responsible legislation.
First and most important are the sections of the legislation which govern the conditions and the rates for newspapers and periodicals. In the revision of the act, the statutory rate for the mailing of newspapers and periodicals is restricted to newspapers and periodicals which meet the new definition of a Canadian newspaper and of a Canadian periodical. The position of the rural newspapers is more clearly defined and the support through postal rates to these little publications is continued. Leaflets, organization publications, house organs and other such material will no longer be classed as second class mail but will be handled at the printed matter or third

September 29, 1967
Post Office Act
class rate. Publications which do not qualify as Canadian will come out of the second class statutory rates category.
With the passing of these sections the revenues from second class mail will be increased but, what is more important, the legislation governing this class of mail will be improved so that the administration of this part of the act will be more defensible and handling costs can be more readily apportioned to the various categories of publications for the purpose of determining postage rates.
The second major item is the increase in postage for first class mail or, as it is more commonly known, letter mail. The new rate on a letter for delivery within the postal area in which it is posted will be five cents for the first ounce or fraction of an ounce and three cents for each additional ounce or fraction of an ounce. The rate on a letter posted within one postal area for delivery in another postal area will be six cents for the first ounce or fraction of an ounce and four cents for each additional ounce or fraction of an ounce.
Concurrently with this rate change it is intended, in accordance with the authority granted under Section 6 of the Post Office Act, to abolish the domestic air mail letter rate and to provide air transmission for all domestic mail prepaid at the first class rate of postage, regardless of weight, providing delivery will be expedited.
Since 1954, only first class mail weighing up to eight ounces has received the all-up service which, by the way, is a postal service Canada pioneered. Now with this change, all first class mail in Canada will receive the all-up service. To business houses across the nation this will be welcome news because the ambiguity which existed between first class all-up and first class air mail will be eliminated. All first class mail in Canada will receive air transport at the one rate.
The change will also raise additional revenues to meet the increased costs and to help reduce the overall post office deficit, which is a factor in current operations.
The third change governs mail transportation arrangements. It reflects a modern day appreciation of the need for flexibility in making contractual arrangements and more equitable adjustments in payments to contractors.
The fourth revision deals with the general administration of the postal operation whereby it is necessary to give authorization to employees to administer oaths and receive affidavits, and where a more lucid statement

of authority is required for the Postmaster General to maintain a continuing group of post office investigators.
I will not elaborate further on the bill because it is very urgent that the bill be presented to the house. I want to assure the committee that when we study the bill, either on second reading or in the clause by clause stage, I will be able to provide the necessary information and answer all the questions asked. However, I think it is very urgent that this bill be presented as soon as possible and made public so as to allay the grave doubts which may be in the minds of the printers of newspapers and periodicals. As soon as the bill is presented, I will be able to provide to the house more information than I can now at the resolution stage.

speechtext: The minister should have given us more information with regard to revenues and expenditures.

speechtext:
I will be able to give the house more specific information with regard to revenues and deficits. As everyone knows, deficits on second class mail have increased substantially in the last two years while first class mail has always shown a profit. However, as hon. members will observe in the next estimates of my department, first class mail is starting to show a deficit. If the rate is increased on first class mail, it will not only cover the deficit in the first class mail and increase first class service but also cover some of the deficit in other classes of mail. Some people might say that those who will be most affected by the increase in the rate on first class mail will be the average citizen writing a few letters a month, but I should like to point out, and this may come as a surprise to many hon. members, that 75 per cent of all first class mail comes from business companies.
I think it will be much easier for hon. members and for the public in general to understand all the details of this bill when it is presented because the regulations and all they entail are very complicated. They are difficult even for post office employees to understand. I think hon. members will find there will be some substantial changes in second class mail.

I should like to ask the minister a question for clarification. At the beginning of his statement he mentioned there were four main changes in the proposal. The first change involved newspapers and periodicals, the second one referred to an increase in first

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the minister for his words of explanation, particularly in connection with first section to which he referred, although perhaps he was not as explicit as I should have liked him to be at this time. However, as he suggested, we will look at this matter very closely when we proceed to the second reading of the bill.
[DOT] (5:40 p.ra.)
I must say at the outset that this is a most shocking resolution to put before this committee, particularly this week since it comes on the heels of recent announcements that point up the woeful mismanagement of affairs in this country. I refer to the admission by the government that the wheat agreement was allowed to lapse and the poor taxpayer will now be called upon to subsidize western wheat, an unnecessary circumstance in the first place. Following on the heels of this avoidable misfortune, the government then suggested that per cent mortgage money was the only way to finance the building of houses.
Three times and out is a familiar cliche, Mr. Chairman, and we have now been presented with the third time. The poor defenceless public now has to face a 20 to 25 per cent hike in postal rates. And for what, Mr. Chairman? I submit it is for curtailed service in many instances and chiefly because of government mismanagement.
Let me say immediately that the poor Postmaster General alone is not responsible for this, because he does try to do his best. But just to prove how things have deteriorated in this country in the past three months, Mr. Chairman, let me refer to an extract from Hansard. As reported at page 1098 for June 2, 1967 the Postmaster General said:
I can tell hon. members that at the five-cent rate for letters we still make money. At four cents we still make some money, although we are on the verge of losing.
Three months later, Mr. Chairman, the minister is saying, in effect, that we are losing money on first class mail, which indicates a pretty rapid deterioration.
Post Office Act
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that much of this resolution is couched in the vaguest of generalities. Nevertheless, the general public is going to be gouged again. The citizens of this country are being called upon, in effect, to subsidize the second class mail operations of the post office. How much more of this inflated cost of doing business, this inflated cost of living, can the Canadian public accept and still survive? We are being forced time and time again to dig deeper and deeper into our pockets, and I suggest that the people of Canada cannot take many more weeks like the past one.
As reported on the same page of Hansard, the minister went on to say in reference to second and third class mail charges:
At the second and third class rates we are losing about $30 million a year.
I suggest there should be more specific reference in this resolution to how the really serious difficulties of financing and operating the post office are going to be resolved. At this juncture we have no idea whether the rates to be attached to the losing part of the operation, that is second and third class mail, are being increased at all. Are they going to be increased proportionately more than the increases applied to that segment of the operation that is self-supporting? According to the statement of the Postmaster General last June, certain elements of his department's operations are profitable. Are rates for second class mail to be reduced?
I do not wish to sound facetious, Mr. Chairman, and I do not intend to be facetious, but my point is this. The resolution refers to increasing by one cent the postage rates for letters posted in Canada for delivery in Canada, and to providing an amended rate structure for newspapers and periodicals. What does "an amended rate structure" mean? Is the rate structure to be amended upwards or downwards? The minister has not spelt that out in the house. The only information we have about post office affairs is in some press releases; but, all we have to go on in this house is the resolution.
Now, Mr. Chairman, if I were a suspicious person, which I assure you I am not, I might assume the word "amended" meant to make a minor change in second class rates, and an attempt to shore up the balance sheet by overcharging the unorganized general public. By "unorganized" I refer to those not represented by strong association lobbies, unlike the publishers. I refer to a body akin, say, to the Manufacturers' Association, which speaks

September 29, 1967
Post Office Act
for its members; and I am assuming, Mr. Chairman, that there must be a newspaper and magazine publishers association.
Incidentally, Mr. Chairman, there is no reference in the resolution to third class mail. I would compliment the post office for the nice way they have of describing the junk that you and I as householders receive in our mailbox almost daily. I refer to advertisements for everything from magazine subscriptions to soap and detergents. Yes, periodically we even receive material from political parties. But there is not a word in the resolution about this segment of the mail.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR INCREASES IN POSTAL RATES, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member realizes that Christmas cards come under third class mail?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR INCREASES IN POSTAL RATES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, but we do not know how large of a deficit is accumulated as a result of this particular segment of the operation of his department.
Another point that causes me concern is this. The resolution commences:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Post Office Act to increase by one cent the postage rates for letters posted in Canada for delivery in Canada;-
That means there must be an international agreement or something on postal rates to which Canada must adhere, and therefore we are powerless to change the rate until another postal convention agreement is signed. I have no idea when such a convention will be convened, and from what the minister said this spring I believe the present agreement has some considerable time to run. This further points up how rapidly our internal conditions have deteriorated.
May I just refer to the United States postal rates for first class mail. Although as of this morning there had been no change, there has been some suggestion that their five cent letter rate will be changed in the not too distant future. But the charge made for third class mail is almost the same as for first class mail. Obviously, the United States authorities have concluded that if advertisers find it profitable to do so, they will continue to use this service. The United States post office is not asking the general public to subsidize that service, and this is as it should be.
I should just like to refer to the London Free Press, an issue of recent date. The article states that the post office committee in the United States has brought in a new bill which provides for a 21 per cent rate boost for second class mail.

[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
This would take effect gradually over a period of three years. Current United States rates on second class mail, including newspapers and magazines, are 4 cents for the first two ounces and 1 cent for each additional ounce. This is the point I was making. The only people who face increases spelled out exactly for them in this country are the little people, the ordinary citizens who do not have huge lobbies working for them.
The rest of the resolution calls for changes in the administration of the act, more especially in relation to tenders and contracts. We have suggested that certain procedures should be changed in this area over the years and we shall look with interest to find out whether some of these suggestions have been included. But I think it is now time that we came to grips with the ever increasing problem of the cost of living. Here is another classic example of the inability of the government to deal satisfactorily with the financial affairs of this country.
It may be said that one cent is a small amount, and I admit that it is. But the principle here is wrong, the principle that the little people of the country should have their burdens spelled out in unmistakable terms while we are not nearly so emphatic where strong organizations are concerned.
I commend the United States post office committee which has looked at this problem from all angles. Traditionally their second class rates have been higher than ours, but they have spelled out what their increase will be. I notice the minister shaking his head. I hope he is shaking it in agreement.
May I conclude by recalling what the minister said on July 2, 1967. At that time he said because our rates are a little lower than rates in the United States and because we have a better service, many magazines printed in the United States are brought into Canada by truck for mailing here. If United States rates go up proportionately more than our own, I submit we shall have quite a line-up of trucks at the border and I wonder how much we shall lose on this operation.
I should like to make the strongest plea at my command to the government that before the second reading of this bill the whole matter be referred to a committee of the house for the closest scrutiny. I suggest that in this way, with a new, non-partisan, constructive approach to our problems, we could help the government arrange a much more satisfactory solution.
September 29, 1967

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR INCREASES IN POSTAL RATES, ETC.
speechtext: I do not rise with the intention of making a speech but to ask a question. Our attitude toward this proposal to increase the rate on first class mail will obviously be influenced by the proposals which the minister has in mind with regard to second class mail. Why can the minister not give this information to the committee so that we may be in a better position to judge the virtues of the other proposal. He has spelled out the increase in the first class rate. Why not for the second class rate.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR INCREASES IN POSTAL RATES, ETC.
speechtext:
The question of increases in rates for second class mail is more complicated than an increase in the cost of first class mail. Obviously we cannot increase rates by less than one cent, because we cannot begin issuing stamps of, say, half a cent denomination. Thus the increase in the cost of first class mail has to be one cent.
As far as second class mail is concerned there are many other factors that can be considered, various directions in which increases can be made, some paying a little more and others, possibly, a little less. As far as daily newspapers are concerned, they are now paying two and a half cents a pound for news and four cents a pound for advertising. The increase on the advertising portion will be bigger.
Some of the magazines or newspapers now enjoying second class statutory rates will cease to have the benefit of these rates because we are working out a new definition of a Canadian newspaper or a Canadian periodical. The result will be, in effect, an increase of more than the one cent. Under the new definition of a weekly newspaper, a weekly newspaper will be a rural paper with a publication figure of less than 10,000. Newspapers with circulation of more than 10,000 will come into another category; there are free zones for the weeklies, and all sorts of arrangements, but I can tell you that there will be increases in second class mail rates.
We are starting right now to have a deficit on first class mail. Our estimates forecast, with regard to the first class, indicates a deficit of over $5 million right now. I can tell hon. members that next year the deficit will be up to $7.7 million, and costs are continuing to rise. In these circumstances, do hon. members opposite not feel it is time to raise the rates?
Whenever we come to increase the salaries of our personnel we are told the amount offered is not enough. We need revenues.
Post Office Act
Transportation costs have risen. There has been no increase in second class rates since 1951, I believe, and no increase in first class rates since 1954.
The hon. member who had just made his speech suggested that the ordinary citizen would have to pay the bulk of the revenue to be provided by this increase. Let me tell him that the average citizen spends on first class mail service of the post office $1.82 a year; the increase will bring this up to $2.19, so the ordinary citizen will be paying 37 cents a year more. But consider the position of the Bell Telephone Company, for example, which has telephones in every home and sends a bill to every house once a month. What about companies and corporations of this kind? It is they who will really be carrying the burden.
I shall have many explanations to give, Mr. Chairman, when the bill is before us and I think it is important that we should come to that stage as soon as possible.

speechtext: If the minister cannot give us details of the increases in the second class rates, can he not indicate the amount which the new rates will provide? I understand that the deficit on second class mail is about $28 million. Does the minister plan to increase revenues by that amount?
